analysis.one_liner: Requires the Education Department to share student loan data with the consumer financial watchdog.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have forced the Education Department to open its student loan files to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and locked that cooperation into loan-servicer contracts, died in committee without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Education to turn over student loan information to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau whenever the bureau's student loan ombudsman asked for it. It would also have barred the Education Department from signing servicing contracts unless the contractor agreed to answer CFPB requests, re-established cooperation agreements between the two agencies that had been terminated, and ordered the CFPB to keep enough staff on its oversight and enforcement units. The aim was to give the bureau the data it needs to police student loan servicers and lenders accused of mistreating borrowers. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 43 million Americans holding student loans, who would gain a watchdog with real access to servicing data; the bill's own findings cite $750 million recovered for defrauded students and $60 million returned to overcharged service members under past CFPB student-loan work.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Education Department's student loan ombudsman to provide student loan information to the CFPB Director or CFPB ombudsman on request.
Bars the Education Department from contracting with a student loan servicer unless that contractor agrees to provide information to the CFPB when asked.

Keeps the 2011 and 2014 information-sharing agreements between the CFPB and Education Department in effect, prohibits unilateral termination, and requires a report on any memoranda changed or rescinded after November 24, 2017.
Directs the CFPB Director to ensure each supervisory and enforcement unit is sufficiently staffed to carry out its duties.

analysis.who_pays: Student loan servicing companies, for-profit colleges, and lenders, which would face a federal consumer bureau with access to their records and contracts; the CFPB's additional staffing would be funded by the bureau's existing financing mechanism.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student loan servicers and for-profit colleges

drawbacks.text: Adding a second policing agency to student loan servicing can duplicate the Education Department's own contractor oversight, and servicers warned of compliance costs that could be passed to borrowers.
Mandating staffing levels for CFPB enforcement units without new appropriations leaves the burden on the agency's own funding, which critics of the bureau argue lacks accountability to Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core exchange is straightforward: borrowers get a consumer watchdog with the data to catch servicer abuses, while the servicing industry absorbs oversight and compliance costs. The bill is modest in scale, so the stakes for any one party are limited, but for a market of roughly $1.5 trillion in outstanding loans, even a modest information-sharing requirement meaningfully shifts the balance toward borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Education and Labor and Financial Services committees in May 2019, and neither committee ever reported it out or gave it any vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Katie Porter introduced the bill on May 17, 2019, with seven original cosponsors, citing $750 million recovered for defrauded students and $60 million returned to overcharged service members by the CFPB's student loan office.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor and, in addition, to the Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote appears in the complete action history before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill finished with 12 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan servicers and lenders avoided a contractual requirement to answer to the CFPB, and borrowers did not get the added oversight; the House majority, which never brought the bill past its committees, also kept a low-cost item off its agenda.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan servicers; borrowers got nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, but all 12 cosponsors were Democrats, none of the 197 House Republicans supported it, and the bills it built on grew out of a 2011-2014 Democratic-era consumer bureau framework.

industries.note: Servicing contractors would have been barred from federal contracts unless they agreed to answer CFPB information requests, exposing them to enforcement built on their own records. The Education Department's own inspector general had reported frequent contractor noncompliance in servicing.

The bill aimed to keep the CFPB's student loan enforcement unit staffed and its data pipelines open, the office that the bill's findings credit with shutting down predatory for-profit colleges and recovering $750 million for defrauded students. More CFPB capacity means more enforcement exposure for these firms.

industries.industry: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (as an institution)
industries.note: The bill required adequate staffing of the bureau's supervisory and enforcement units and locked in its interagency information-sharing agreements, insulating the bureau's student loan work from future administrative rollbacks.
